title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 3: Microchips, Modems and Media Invade Mount Olympus
keywords: Microchips, Modems and Media Invade Mount Olympus
Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's lecture asking 'how have microchips, modems and media affected life on Mount Olympus?', organized around cyber technology's impact on legal doctrines, on judicial tools, and on the Court's relationship with its publics.

The doctrinal challenge of the Third Wave: Toffler's three civilizations, the AOL-Time Warner merger, Amazon.com and Bill Gates as evidence of an information economy, and the unanswered questions posed by e-commerce, telemedicine, surrogate parenthood, cloning, e-economics and e-media.

The Court's technological response: a Committee on Computerization and the MISO, the Case Administration System, Computer-Assisted Legal Research, computerized administrative processes, the Internet homepage and 1,500 computers, with speech recognition, paperless communication, information kiosks and video teleconferencing planned.

The four options for confronting media criticism -- surrender, silence, all-out combat, or professional help -- and his argument that transparency and accountability, embodied in the Davide Watch and the Public Information Office, are the Court's best response, coupled with a plea for discreet restraint from journalists.
sub_topics: He frames the lecture's three topics and its guiding question about Mount Olympus.

Toffler's The Third Wave divides civilization into agricultural, industrial and information phases, the last of which 'will topple bureaucracies, reduce the role of the nation-state' and require simpler, more effective yet more democratic governments.

He admits that twenty years earlier he could not imagine information outvaluing food and machines, but the personal computer, the Internet and the dotcom revolution have proved that 'knowledge is power.'

Three proofs: the $162-billion AOL absorption of Time Warner creating a $350-billion conglomerate -- 22 times the Philippine budget for 2000; Amazon.com as the earth's biggest seller owning no store, its 35-year-old Jeff Bezos named Time's Person of the Year; and America's and Bill Gates's primacy resting on information technology, with even Sony betting on Playstation 2.

Doctrinal puzzles on e-commerce: whether a bare computer order is a contract of sale, whether paperless communication is admissible, who is liable for a misdelivered left-hand-drive car, where suit may be filed, and whether an Internet-transmitted pleading is acceptable.

Puzzles on telemedicine: whether an e-medical company practices medicine illegally here, who answers for a fatal misdiagnosis, and where suits should be filed; and on surrogate parenthood and cloning: who the legal parents are, and whether a person may patent himself or regenerate tissue commercially.

On e-economics, he asks whether liberalization and globalization shift threats to civil liberties from government to market forces, citing Tanada v. Angara upholding WTO membership, Tatad v. Secretary of Energy nullifying RA 8180 and Garcia v. Corona validating RA 8479.

On e-media, ABS-CBN v. Commission on Elections held exit polls and their dissemination essential parts of free speech and beyond Comelec's power to ban -- a ruling his staff could find no counterpart to in any other credible Supreme Court.

Vasquez v. Court of Appeals made truth a complete defense in libel involving a public official and imported the actual-malice standard, reversing jurisprudence that required the accused to prove absence of malice.

The Court's e-tools: the Committee on Computerization once chaired by Justice Davide and now by Justice Melo with CJP as vice-chair, and the MISO under Atty. Ivan John Enrile Uy 'with a full-time staff of computer geeks.'

The systems themselves: the Case Administration System tracking cases from filing to disposal, Computer-Assisted Legal Research compiling all decisions from 1901 and eventually doing away with the SCRA and Philippine Reports, computerized payrolls and records, the Internet homepage, 1,500 computers for the trial courts, and Philja's computer training.

Planned innovations within Chief Justice Davide's term: voice or speech recognition in place of stenography, electronic data interchange of orders, writs and pleadings, electronic information kiosks for case calendars, and video teleconferencing to spare detainees, handicapped witnesses and traumatized victims.

He recalls a past in which courts were sacrosanct, justices 'treated like little deities on Mount Olympus,' magistrates living 'in hermetic isolation' under a vow of silence, and no credible journalist daring to lampoon the Court.

That enclave has been invaded: media cameras 'dangled as new, effective and efficient tools for processing truth,' a generation of Filipinos thirty and under making up 70 percent of the population and schooled to challenge authority, and a post-EDSA libertarian spirit -- a phenomenon shared with the US, Britain, Continental Europe and Australia, as Justice Michael Kirby observed.

The four options, named in Filipino: 'Una, sumuko agad' -- caving in, which abdicates the judicial function; 'Pangalawa, magmatigas at huwag pansinin' -- silence behind Lincoln's line, which the public reads as an admission of guilt; 'Pangatlo, lumaban nang puspusan' -- fighting back, risky because jurists lack the aptitude for media battles; and 'Pang-apat, magpatulong sa marunong' -- the option the Court chose, creating the Committee on Public Information he chairs and the Public Information Office under Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr.

Transparency and accountability as the best response, quoting the Davide Watch that the Bench 'must be fully accountable to the people by remaining transparent' without betraying what requires confidentiality.

Evidence of that policy: an eighteen-month nationwide consultation with UNDP and NEDA hearing more than a thousand individuals, producing the 'Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary' launched February 4, 2000; a February 18, 2000 dialogue with business leaders; and a March 3, 2000 World Bank-assisted 'Consultation-Workshop to Identify Judicial Reform Priorities.'

He explains his own conduct as part of that policy -- chairing the Committee on Public Information, shedding his vow of silence to speak, and writing one book a year 'to open a new window to the Court.'
He welcomes scrutiny of incompetent or corrupt judges and fair comment on decisions objectively presented, but will not countenance baseless attacks on jurists' person, honor, dignity or motives.

The plea for discreet restraint: judges generally cannot answer back effectively, are not politicians who court the limelight, and can be permanently damaged by wanton attacks -- yet the Court depends on public trust, commanding neither army nor police nor money for patronage.

The epilogue's partnership thesis: media and judiciary are 'natural partners' bound by the search for truth, the protection of rights and the defense of society's norms, both lacking coercive resources and appealing only to reason -- and a closing plea to help uphold the judiciary as 'the last bulwark of democracy.'

stances.claim: The information revolution has irreversibly altered life on Mount Olympus, and the judiciary must adjust -- and adjust speedily -- to the doctrinal challenges posed by e-commerce, telemedicine, genetic technology, globalized markets and electronic media.
stances.rhetorical_move: Toffler-derived framing plus a catalogue of unanswered hypotheticals that dramatize the doctrinal gap

stances.claim: Caving in to popular pressure would be an abdication of the judicial function, because a litigation is won not by cheers from the gallery but by reasoned arguments based on legal principles and precedents.
stances.rhetorical_move: option-by-option elimination, each named in Filipino and dispatched in turn

stances.claim: Silence is self-defeating, since silence -- worse, bullheadedness -- is normally read by the public as an admission of guilt, and an unreasonable refusal to answer prima facie criticism erodes public trust.
stances.rhetorical_move: consequence argument that turns a traditional judicial virtue into an institutional risk

stances.claim: Transparency and accountability are the Court's best response to media criticism; the Court has therefore chosen professional public information help rather than surrender, silence or combat.
stances.rhetorical_move: fourth-option resolution supported by the Davide Watch text and a record of consultations and workshops

stances.claim: Scrutiny of incompetent or corrupt judges and fair comment on objectively presented decisions are welcome, but baseless attacks on a jurist's person, honor, dignity or alleged motives will not be countenanced.
stances.rhetorical_move: concession-then-limit, drawing a line between accountability and defamation

stances.claim: Media and the judiciary are natural partners, bound by the same search for truth and the same lack of coercive power, so journalists should exercise discreet restraint toward judges who generally cannot answer back.
stances.rhetorical_move: partnership peroration built on a symmetry of purposes and of weaknesses

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' is Panganiban's lecture asking how microchips, modems and media have affected life on Mount Olympus, organized around three impacts of cyber technology. Invoking Alvin Toffler's The Third Wave, he argues that the information phase is transforming everything, citing the $162-billion AOL absorption of Time Warner, Amazon.com and its Person-of-the-Year founder Jeff Bezos, and Bill Gates's fortune built on compressing knowledge into microchips. He then catalogues doctrinal puzzles the judiciary is unready for: whether a bare computer order is a contract of sale and where suit lies for a misdelivered car; whether an e-medical company practices medicine illegally and who answers for a fatal misdiagnosis; who the legal parents of a surrogate child are and whether a person may patent himself; whether globalization shifts threats to liberty from government to markets, as in Tanada v. Angara, Tatad v. Secretary of Energy and Garcia v. Corona; and the media rulings in ABS-CBN v. Comelec, protecting exit polls, and Vasquez v. Court of Appeals, importing actual malice. Second, he inventories the Court's response: a Committee on Computerization and the MISO, the Case Administration System, Computer-Assisted Legal Research covering decisions from 1901, computerized administrative processes, the Court's website, 1,500 computers for trial courts, and planned speech recognition, electronic data interchange, information kiosks and video teleconferencing. Third, he describes how a once-sacrosanct bench, whose justices were 'treated like little deities,' now faces a questioning post-EDSA generation and an invasive press. Of four options -- surrender, silence, combat or professional help -- the Court chose the fourth, creating the Committee on Public Information he chairs. He closes on transparency and accountability, welcoming fair scrutiny but pleading for discreet restraint, since 'the media and the judiciary are natural partners.'
